$comment: COACH ME, rebuilt twice on 2026-09-11. Morning: his complaint that there was not much there he could
use, so the tab opened on his own stroke counts and the checks became Do and Check cards.
AFTERNOON, on his own report of how he swims, in his words: the 450 ended on breathing and arms; the
400 was a set he chose after getting out to rest; he does the high elbow and still cannot feel his
lats; pressing the chest makes him dip like a small dive; the hum works but the internet disagrees
about how much to breathe out; he cannot find rotation or the kick from the hips; he wants questions
to ask himself mid-swim, things to do on land, and drills that fit a public lane. Every one of those
is answered below from US Masters Swimming's own pages, several of them already captured: the pull
guide says the catch is a reposition and the hand speeds up through the pull; the breathing guide
says slow exhale then a final forceful one; the body position guide says the shoulders lead the
roll; and both guides carry dryland work, including a cord squeeze written as a learning tool for
feeling the back muscles. Each Check reads as a question he can answer in the water.
SOURCES ARE US MASTERS SWIMMING ONLY, his ruling of 2026-09-02. The research on where to put your
attention while swimming (Freudenheim and colleagues 2010) is a study, not a USMS page, so it is a
cue on the How tab rather than a card here. Every quote is checked against content/swim/sources/
yourWords is what HE reported about a piece, which only he can know. It renders beside that piece's
trace. Add a row when he says how one ended; never write one for him.

yourWords.said: Tired, mostly: breathing and arms together.
A set you chose, after getting out to rest. You could have kept going, and stopped because your form would have slipped.

items.name: One thing per swim
items.do: Before you get in, pick one card below. Think only about that one, and ask its question every few lengths. Keep the same card until it happens without thinking.
items.check: After the swim, can you name the one thing you worked on, and was its answer yes more often at the end than at the start?

quotes.text: Take your time as you swim to think about just that one thing. It's easy to get lost in all the technical details. Picking one at a time means you can narrow it down and focus on change.
It's going to take repeated, focused drills over time to make a lasting correction to your stroke.

items.name: The catch is a reposition, not the pull
items.do: From the stretch, drop the hand down and in while the elbow bends out to the side. Smooth and easy: you are turning the forearm to face back, not pulling yet.
items.check: Was the catch the easy part? If it felt like the hard part, you started pulling before the forearm faced back.

quotes.text: Your catch doesn't involve grabbing or holding water; it's simply repositioning your arm in preparation for creating propulsion with an effective pull.
The action should be smooth and the change in position shouldn't require much effort. Think about repositioning as opposed to actively pulling.

items.name: Speed the hand up through the pull
items.do: Once the forearm faces back, push the water straight back and let the hand get faster toward your hip. On a long piece, start slow and finish slightly faster.
items.check: Is my hand moving faster at my hip than it was at the catch?

quotes.text: Increase your hand speed throughout your pull. When attempting to sprint, start with a high hand speed and get faster; if you're doing a distance swim, start much slower and end slightly faster on your pull.
Your primary focus should be on pulling and pushing directly backward.

items.name: Hand and forearm, one paddle
items.do: Keep the hand and forearm facing back together, elbow out to the side, for as long as the pull lasts. The feel of the back muscles behind it is easier to learn on land: the cord squeeze at the bottom.
items.check: Is the pressure along my forearm too, or only in my palm?

quotes.text: To pull effectively, have your hand and forearm facing backward.
Once you've created a large surface area, your goal should be to maintain the same surface area as long as possible throughout your pull.

items.name: Finish past the hip, then back and up
items.do: Finish just past your hip, and in the last part pull back and up so the arm swings straight into the recovery. The very end is small muscles, so do not force it.
items.check: Does my hand brush my thigh, and does the arm leave the water without a stall?

quotes.text: your hands should finish your pull just past your hips. Your arm should not be completely straight at this point.
during the last part of your pulling phase, think about pulling back and up, rather than just straight back.

Because there's very little surface area moving backward at this point (just your hand) and the muscles performing the work are relatively small (just your triceps), you won't create much propulsion, however.

items.name: Pull harder, keep the kick going
items.do: When you work on the pull, keep the legs kicking. A harder pull sinks the hips, and the kick is what holds them up.
items.check: When I focus on the pull, do my legs start to drag?

quotes.text: For instance, the beginning of your pull causes your hips to sink, and the harder you pull, the more your hips sink. A strong kick counteracts this sinking effect.

items.name: Breathe out slowly, then blow the rest just before you turn
items.do: Face in: let the air out slowly, like a hum, keeping some in to float on. Just before you turn to breathe, one hard blow to empty. Then the breath in is quick.
items.check: When my mouth clears the water, is the only thing left to do breathe in?

quotes.text: After inhaling and returning your head to the water, patiently and slowly exhale. There is no urgency to this action, and it does not need to be forceful. Just prior to breathing in again, perform a final, forceful exhalation during which your lungs are cleared of air.
Exhale as you swim, letting air out slowly as if you're humming.
The stronger the buoyant force, the less work that needs to be done to maintain a proper body position in the water.

items.name: Lean on your chest, and hold the lean
items.do: From the push-off, lean your head and chest into the water and keep that lean the whole length. A lean is a position you hold, not a push on every stroke.
items.check: Is the lean steady from wall to wall, or do I dip on each stroke? A dip every stroke means ease off and hold it.

quotes.text: The first strategy is to press your head and chest, the lighter end of the seesaw, down into the water.
By leaning into the water and leaning into your lungs, you'll put pressure into the flotation you feel in your chest.

items.name: Firm the back of your body
items.do: If the lean is not enough, tighten your lower back, glutes and the backs of your legs together. The superman on the land cards is the same feeling on the floor.
items.check: Do my heels feel close to the surface?

quotes.text: Some swimmers also need to think about creating tension in their lower back and legs to lift their hips and legs.
Your lower back and hips are key for creating tension in the back of your body. This tension holds your legs up at the surface of the water, preventing them from sinking.

items.name: Shoulders lead the roll, hips follow
items.do: Let the shoulders start the roll and the hips come with them, spine straight, no twist at the waist. Roll only as far as your arm needs to clear the water.
items.check: Does my arm swing over the water without dragging? If it drags, roll more. If it clears, that is enough.

quotes.text: The role of rotation is to allow for extra range of motion in your shoulders, so your shoulders should lead the rotation.

If you're unable to recover your arms smoothly over the surface, you need to rotate more. Once you can rotate your arms smoothly over the surface, that amount of rotation is sufficient and more would be counterproductive.
Rotation only works if you keep your spine relatively straight. Your whole spine needs to rotate in the same way at the same time for your rotation to fulfill its function.

items.name: Small, fast kick
items.do: Keep the kick small and quick, feet under the surface.
items.check: Is there air on the soles of my feet? There should not be.

quotes.text: Kicking is expensive. It takes a lot of energy to produce speed with your legs, and a big kick takes a lot more energy than a smaller kick.

items.name: The kick starts at the hip
items.do: Hip first, knee second, ankle third, like a whip.
items.check: You cannot see this from inside the water. A phone on the deck filming one length is the only way to know.

quotes.text: Your down-kick begins at your hip, your knee moves second, and your ankle moves third.
Use videos of yourself swimming and mental pictures or words to help you understand the change you're trying to make.

items.name: Count your strokes on every length
items.do: Count stroke cycles on one arm, every length of the long piece.
items.check: Is this length two or more above my usual count? Then it cost more than it should have, whatever it felt like.

quotes.text: Counting your strokes is a measure of swimming efficiency. The fewer strokes you can take, the more efficiently you're swimming.

items.name: Turn without standing up
items.do: Touch with one hand, knees to your chest, roll back, feet on the wall, twist off it as you push.
items.check: Eight walls in a row without a foot on the floor, on an easy swim, before you use it in the long piece.

quotes.text: Open turns for freestyle are like open turns for butterfly and breaststroke in terms of how to do them. The only difference is that you only use one hand to touch the wall instead of two.
The most important movement in an open turn is aggressively bringing your knees to your chest and then rolling backward.
As you push off, twist off the wall, just as if you were going to jump and twist on land while jumping up.
Don't use your turns as an opportunity to rest; instead, use them as an opportunity to gain an advantage.

items.name: Arrive on a full stroke
items.do: Adjust your stroke three or four cycles out so you reach the wall on a full stroke.
items.check: Did I touch on a full reach, with no glide in and no short chopped stroke?

quotes.text: Start adjusting your stroke three or four cycles from the wall to ensure you hit the wall on a full stroke.

items.name: Wall pull, at the end of the lane
items.do: At the wall, hands and forearms flat on the deck at pull width. Press down with the whole arm to lift yourself a little, lower, a few times. Then swim a length looking for the same pressure.
items.check: Could I feel the pressure along the whole forearm, and find it again in the length after?

quotes.text: The goal is to focus on creating pressure with your whole arm, as well as experimenting with different positions of your arm.
place your hands and forearms on the surface of the pool deck at approximately the width and angle of your arm pull
Each series of drills is followed by a freestyle repetition to practice these skills during the goal movement of freestyle.

items.name: Fists, then open hands
items.do: Swim one length with tight fists, then one with open hands. It looks like normal swimming, so it fits any lane.
items.check: On the open-hand length, do I feel the water on my palm and forearm more?

quotes.text: By closing your fists, you're forced to better integrate your forearm into your pull to compensate for the smaller surface area pushing against the water. This helps you learn to use all the surface area that your arm provides. Furthermore, when you reopen your hands, it's much easier to feel the water.

items.name: The catch, standing up
items.do: One arm straight up. Turn the hand down while the elbow bends out to the side, then back. Ten slow ones, at home or at the wall between lengths.
items.check: Does the elbow stay high while the hand drops?

quotes.text: Rotate your hand down while simultaneously bending your elbow to the side.
You can practice this movement anywhere, including while resting between repetitions during a workout.

items.name: Cord squeeze: learn to feel your back
items.do: Band anchored high in front. Straight arms, pull down to your hips, hold 3 to 5 seconds, let it back up. Hard but manageable. On a pull-down at the gym, the same finish: elbows into your ribs.
items.check: Do I feel it in my back, below the armpits, rather than in my arms?

quotes.text: The purpose of this exercise is to help you feel the contraction of the strong muscles of your back. These muscles are most effective at creating a powerful pull.
This is less of a strength exercise and more of a learning tool. It can help increase your awareness of how to use these muscles. That awareness can help you pull more effectively in the water.
With straight arms, pull against the cord and bring your hands down to your hips. Hold that position for 3-5 seconds.
Focus on squeezing your elbows to your torso to determine your range of motion.

items.name: Alternating superman: the back of the body
items.do: On your stomach, arms forward. Squeeze your back and glutes, lift one arm and the opposite leg, hold a moment, switch.
items.check: Do my glutes and lower back switch on together? That is the tension that lifts your legs in the water.

quotes.text: Alternating Superman improves your ability to create tension on the back of your body while also developing strength and endurance to maintain these skills.
Squeeze the muscles of your back and hips and lift one arm and the opposite leg off the ground.

items.name: Rolling elbow plank: the roll without a bend
items.do: From a plank on your elbows, roll onto one elbow with the body in one straight line, back to both, then the other side.
items.check: Did I roll as one piece, or bend at the waist?

quotes.text: Rolling elbow plank allows you to practice that skill on land while also developing the muscles responsible for ensuring it happens in the water. The key is for your movement to be purely rotational, rather than a bend at your waist.
